food.text: Ottoman cuisine grew out of long-term interaction among culinary traditions from Central Asia, the Persian and Arab region, Byzantium, and the empire's Balkan and Anatolian lands. Food historians stress exchange, adaptation and regional variation rather than a single line of influence.

When Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, the Turks gained control of the spice trade in the eastern Mediterranean. Spices went into health tonics made by the palace confectionery, which could be eaten as sweets and could contain up to 60 different spices.

Mantı, a dumpling dish especially associated with Kayseri in Central Anatolia, has cognate names in Chinese, such as mantou, meaning steamed bun. It is generally considered to have originated in Mongolia during the 13th century.

Utskho suneli is a traditional Georgian spice mix made with blue fenugreek, and its name means 'foreign spice'. It is thought to have taken in culinary traditions from the influence of late medieval Persia or Mughal India. Today it appears in almost every Georgian dish.

Historian Maxime Rodinson argued that when similar dishes appear in both eastern and western traditions, one must first ask whether they share a common, parallel origin in Graeco-Roman cooking. In his view Latin Europe, Islam and the Byzantine Empire all shared elements inherited from antiquity.

art.text: Early Ottoman architecture began in northwestern Anatolia around the end of the 13th century. It grew out of earlier Seljuk Turkish architecture, with influences from Byzantine and Iranian architecture. Over the 14th and 15th centuries builders experimented with many building types.

Sultan Kayqubad I, who reigned from 1220 to 1237, is remembered today for his rich architectural legacy and the brilliant court culture of his reign. Later Anatolians often looked back on his time as a golden age.

Three main types of building dominated early Ottoman architecture: single-domed mosques, T-plan buildings and multi-domed buildings. Religious buildings were often part of larger charitable complexes called külliyes, which could include madrasas, hammams, tombs and commercial establishments.

In 1334-1335, Orhan built a mosque in İznik that no longer stands but has been excavated by archeologists. It is the earliest known example of the T-plan, or Bursa-type, mosque, with a central court, often domed, and iwans on three sides.

Several Bursa-type mosques were built in and around Bursa, including the Orhan Gazi Mosque in 1339 and the Yildirim Bayezid I Mosque, completed in 1395. The Hüdavendigar (Murad I) Mosque was built between 1366 and 1385.

The Üç Şerefeli Mosque in Edirne, completed in 1447, has a wide arcaded courtyard leading to a prayer hall dominated by a huge central dome. Its design marked a major step toward the form of later imperial mosques.

After Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453, the first Ottoman imperial mosque in the city was the Fatih Mosque, completed in 1470. Its design showed the growing influence of the ancient Hagia Sophia on Ottoman architects.

The Haji Bektash Veli Complex in central Anatolia was built in the 13th century as a teqe, or dervish lodge, for Haji Bektash Veli, and after his death his mausoleum was added within it. The site later became the pir evi, the spiritual center of the Bektashi Order that he had inspired.
The side iwans and rooms of Bursa-type buildings may have housed Sufi students and traveling dervishes. Sufi brotherhoods were one of the main supporters of the early Ottomans.

The Green Mosque built by Mehmed I between 1412 and 1424 is notable for its extensive tile decoration in the cuerda seca technique. It is the first instance of lavish tile decoration in Ottoman architecture.

In Bursa's central commercial district, Bayezid II ordered a large caravanserai built in 1490-1491, now known as Koza Han. It has a square courtyard with a two-story arched gallery, and a small octagonal mosque stands on raised pillars in its center.

The Kapıağa Medrese in Amasya, built in 1489 by the official Hüseyin Agha, is the only madrasa in Anatolia with an octagonal floor plan. Its design appears similar to the darüşşifa of Bayezid's complex in Edirne, though it is unclear if the architects were related.

The Firuz Ağa Mosque near the Hippodrome in Istanbul dates from 1491. It is small and simple, a square chamber under a single dome, yet its design set an example for many later small mosques in the city.

war.text: Turkic peoples of the Seljuk Empire arrived in Anatolia mainly in the eleventh century. Their Oğuz Turkic tribes made the east of Anatolia a new homeland after the Battle of Manzikert on August 26, 1071. The Seljuks then gradually conquered the Anatolian part of the Byzantine Empire.

On 26 August 1071, a Seljuk army crushed the Byzantine army near Manzikert. The Byzantine right wing was routed, then the left, and the centre, including Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes and the Varangian Guard, was encircled. Romanos was wounded and taken prisoner, and fleeing soldiers were pursued through the night. The emperor's personal troops and the Armenian foot soldiers suffered the heaviest casualties, and by dawn the professional core of the Byzantine army had been destroyed. The defeat undermined Byzantine authority in Anatolia and Armenia and allowed the gradual Turkification of Anatolia.

The Mongols defeated the Seljuk armies at the Battle of Kosedag on 26 June 1243, and the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm became a vassal of the Mongols. The Ilkhanate then ruled Anatolia through Mongol military governors. The last Seljuk sultan, Mesud II, died in 1308.

On 28 July 1402, Timur defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at the Çubuk plain near Ankara. The battle began with a large Ottoman attack that was met by swarms of arrows from the Timurid horse archers; several thousand Ottomans were killed and many surrendered to Timur. Bayezid was captured and died in captivity three months later. The defeat brought almost total collapse of the Ottoman state and a civil war among Bayezid's sons that lasted until 1413.

The Byzantines lost Constantinople in 1453, formally ending the Byzantine-Ottoman wars. Before the final assault the Sultan reminded his troops of the vast wealth and pillaging of the city to come, and an all-out assault captured it on May 29, 1453. Niccolò Barbaro, a Venetian surgeon present at the siege, wrote that all day the Turks made a great slaughter of Christians, that blood flowed in the city like rainwater after a sudden storm, and that the corpses of Turks and Christians were thrown into the Dardanelles. Several Byzantine holdouts lasted until 1479.

Around 1053, Constantine IX disbanded what the historian John Skylitzes called the "Iberian Army", which consisted of 50,000 men. Contemporaries Michael Attaleiates and Kekaumenos agreed that this did catastrophic harm to the empire's eastern defenses. In 1064, a large Seljuk army under Alp Arslan attacked Iberia and took Ani after a siege of 25 days.

During the Battle of Ankara, Timur diverted Çubuk creek, the main water supply of both armies, to a reservoir near the town of Çubuk. This left the Ottoman army with no water. The Ottomans had already marched through the midsummer heat and arrived tired and thirsty, with no time to rest. They were defeated at Catal hill, and Bayezid escaped to the mountains with a few hundred horsemen before Timur surrounded the mountains and captured him.

In 1243, Baiju advanced to Erzurum with Georgian and Armenian warriors under Avag and Shanshe. The city's governor Yakut refused to surrender, so Baiju stormed it with the power of twelve catapults. Sultan Kaykhusraw II then summoned his forces at Konya.

In 1073, at the Battle of the Zompos Bridge near Amorium, Roussel de Bailleul's rebel Norman mercenaries beat the Byzantine army. Roussel had persuaded the Frankish mercenaries on the Byzantine side to defect, and they turned on their own army in mid-battle. John Doukas and his son Andronikos were attacked from two sides, with the river at their backs, and were abandoned when Nikephoros Botaneiates held back the reserve and retreated. Both Doukases were captured. Coming after Manzikert, the defeat left a power vacuum in Asia Minor, and Suleiman ibn Qutalmish led Seljuk Turks in conquering vast swathes of Central Anatolia.

Bursa, the first major town the Ottomans conquered, surrendered under threat of starvation after a long blockade rather than after an assault. Osman's army had not yet developed the means to conduct sieges, and only under Orhan and Murad I did the Ottomans master siege warfare.

Stefan Lazarević and his Serbian knights fought off the Timurid assaults at Ankara and cut through the Mongol ranks three times. Each time Stefan advised Bayezid to break out with him, Bayezid declined. Their heavy black plate armour was very effective against Timurid arrows, and Timur said they "fight like lions".

The fate of Nicaea was sealed when the Byzantine relief army was defeated at Pelekanos on 10 June 1329. Nicaea surrendered in 1331, a massive blow because of its strategic position relative to Constantinople. The Ottomans had already taken Bursa from the Byzantines in 1326.

literature.text: After the Seljuk victory at the Battle of Manzikert in the late 11th century, the Oghuz Turks began to settle in Anatolia. Alongside their older oral traditions, a written literary tradition arose there, drawing its themes, genres and styles largely from Persian literature. For about 900 years the oral and written traditions stayed largely separate.

The earliest known illustrated manuscript in the Persian language is an early 13th century copy of the epic Varka and Golshah. It was most probably created in Konya, under the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, and can be dated to about 1250.

One of the most important figures of early Turkish literature was the 13th century Sufi poet Yunus Emre, dated to 1240? to 1320?. He belongs to the tekke tradition, whose poems were generally meant to be sung in religious gatherings, somewhat like Western hymns (ilahi).

Turkish folk literature extends in a more or less unbroken line from about the 10th or 11th century to today. It has three basic genres: epic, folk poetry and folklore. The dominant element in its folk poetry has always been song.

Turks first became an Islamic people around the 9th or 10th century CE, and religion came to exercise an enormous influence on their society and literature. The mystically oriented Sufi and Shi'a varieties of Islam left a strong mark on Turkish folk poetry.

The poems of the tekke tradition were written down from the very beginning. They were produced by revered religious figures in the literate environment of the tekke. In the aşık/ozan tradition, by contrast, the majority could not read or write.

The aşık/ozan tradition, in which song is the dominant element, is still alive today. It grew up in a milieu where most people could not read or write, unlike the literate tekke, where religious poems were recorded in writing.
The golden age of Ottoman literature began in the 15th century. It consisted mostly of divan poetry, though there were also some prose works.
The Book of Dede Korkut did not fade once the Oghuz Turks had, by and large, settled in Anatolia. It continued to survive in the oral tradition there, passed on by word of mouth.

Süleyman Çelebi, who died in 1422, wrote a highly popular long poem called Vesiletü'n-Necat, meaning "The Means of Salvation". It is more commonly known as the Mevlid and concerns the birth of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.
Kaygusuz Abdal, born in 1397, is widely considered the founder of Alevi/Bektashi literature. He is counted among the major figures of tekke literature, alongside Yunus Emre and Süleyman Çelebi.

Yunus Emre occasionally used Hayran, a riddle-like poetic device inspired by the older Central Asian epic the Book of Dede Korkut. Like that epic, his verses were handed down through a strictly oral tradition before being written down.

In the Battle of Manzikert's aftermath, Norman soldiers who had served in the Byzantine armies spread tales about the defeat. They likely inspired an episode in the Chanson de Roland, in which the amirant of Babylon, Baligant, fights Charlemagne and is defeated only through the aid of Saint Gabriel.

science.text: The first Ottoman hospital, Dar al-Shifa, which literally means "house of health", was built in 1399 in Bursa, the Ottoman capital. Later Ottoman hospitals were structured much like it.
science.source_title: Science and technology in the Ottoman Empire

science.text: Ottoman hospitals treated mentally ill patients with music therapy. The patients stayed in separate buildings that were still part of the hospital complex, and different mental illnesses were treated with different modes of music therapy.
science.source_title: Science and technology in the Ottoman Empire

science.text: The musket appeared in the Ottoman Empire by 1465. These large hand-held steel guns were capable of penetrating heavy armor.
science.source_title: Science and technology in the Ottoman Empire

science.text: Ottoman hospitals were structured like those of the Seljuk Empire. In Seljuk hospitals, even wounded crusaders reportedly preferred Muslim doctors because they were very knowledgeable.
science.source_title: Science and technology in the Ottoman Empire

science.text: A hospital established in 1470, the Faith Complex dârüşşifâ, separated patients by sex and used music to treat the mentally ill. It remained open until 1824.
science.source_title: Science and technology in the Ottoman Empire

science.text: The Bâyezîd Dârüşşifâ was founded in 1488 and is best known for its unique architecture. That design influenced the architecture of later European hospitals.
science.source_title: Science and technology in the Ottoman Empire

science.text: Ottoman hospitals were first established and used mainly for treating the sick. They then developed into centers for teaching medical science as well.
science.source_title: Science and technology in the Ottoman Empire

science.text: In the 15th century the Ottomans perfected the musket by creating a gun that used a lever and spring. This design was much easier to use during combat.

politics.text: The Fall of Constantinople in 1453 is seen as the symbolic moment when the emerging Ottoman state shifted from a mere principality into an empire. Sultan Mehmed II, who reigned from 1451 to 1481, had by then accumulated enough personal power to establish a centralized imperial state.

In 1077 the Sultanate of Rum seceded from the Seljuk Empire under Suleiman ibn Qutalmish. Its capital was first at Nicaea and then at Iconium. The name Rum was a synonym for the medieval Roman Empire, and the state is considered the beginning of Turkish history in Anatolia.

After the Seljuk collapse, Anatolia was split among many Turkmen principalities called beyliks. The most powerful were the Karamanids and the Germiyanids in the central area. The Ottoman beylik, around Söğüt in the northwest, was then small and insignificant, but it evolved into the Ottoman Empire over the next 200 years.

Mkhitar Gosh's law code, the Datastanagirk or 'Book of Judgement,' gained the force of law in the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia during the 13th century and was introduced during the reign of the Zakarian princes. It represents one of the major monuments of medieval Armenian legal thought.

In 1241, after Ögedei died, the Seljuk sultan Kaykhusraw II repudiated his vassalage to the Mongols. Baiju demanded that he go to Mongolia in person, give hostages, and accept a Mongol darughachi. When the sultan refused, Baiju declared war, leading to the campaign of 1241–1243 that culminated in the Battle of Köse Dağ.

In the Battle of Ankara in 1402, the Turco-Mongol leader Timur defeated Ottoman forces and took Sultan Bayezid I prisoner, throwing the empire into disorder. A civil war followed from 1402 to 1413 as Bayezid's sons fought over the succession. It ended when Mehmed I emerged as the sultan.

In 1461 Mehmed II joined forces with Kızıl Ahmed Bey, the brother of Ismail, and captured Sinop, officially ending the reign of the Candar dynasty. He first appointed Ahmed Bey governor of Kastamonu and Sinop, but revoked the appointment in 1464.

The Mongol invasion pushed Turkomens to move into western Anatolia, where they founded principalities called beyliks. The Karamanids and Germiyanids were the most powerful in the central area. The Ottoman beylik around Söğüt was then small and insignificant.

In 1048–1049 the Seljuks, commanded by Ibrahim Yinal, uterine brother of Tughril, made their first incursion into the Byzantine frontier region of Iberia. They clashed with a combined Byzantine-Georgian army of 50,000 at the Battle of Kapetron on 10 September 1048. The devastation left the area, in the words of the Byzantine magnate Eustathios Boilas in 1051–1052, "foul and unmanageable... inhabited by snakes, scorpions, and wild beasts". The Arab chronicler Ibn al-Athir wrote that Ibrahim brought back 100,000 captives and 10,000 camel loads of loot.

Under Mongol suzerainty, the Anatolian beyliks did not mint coins in their own leaders' names. Osman I was the first Turkish ruler to do so, in the 1320s. Because Islamic practice gave minting only to a sovereign, this suggests the Ottomans had become independent of the Mongol Khans.

Kaykaus I, the Seljuk sultan of Rum, captured Sinop and made the Empire of Trebizond his vassal in 1214. He also subjugated Cilician Armenia. His father Kaykhusraw I had earlier captured the Mediterranean harbour of Attalia in 1207.

After the Seljuk defeat at Köse Dağ, Hethum I of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia quickly made peace with the Mongols in 1243. In 1247 he sent his brother Sembat to the Mongol court of Karakorum to negotiate an alliance with the Khagan Güyük.

The Ottoman sultan Bayezid I, who reigned from 1389 to 1402, styled himself sultan-ı Rûm, meaning sultan of Rome. Unlike Mehmed II's later Roman ambitions, this was an attempt to claim the legacy of the Sultanate of Rum and challenge the other beyliks in Anatolia.

The Ottoman ruler Osman I was the first Turkish ruler to mint coins in his own name, in the 1320s. Minting was a prerogative of a sovereign in Islamic practice, so this suggests the Ottomans had become independent of the Mongol Khans. The other beyliks had not minted coins in their leaders' names while under Ilkhanid suzerainty.

Kayqubad I acquired the port of Kalon Oros, which was later renamed Ala'iyya in his honor. He also settled Turcomans along the Taurus Mountains frontier, in a region later called İçel. At the end of the 13th century these Turcomans established the Karamanids.

In 1383 Kötürüm Bayezid of the Candar dynasty lost Kastamonu to his own son Süleyman, who had received military support from the Ottoman sultan Murad I. Kötürüm Bayezid retreated to Sinop, which divided the Beylik of Candar. Süleyman reunited it in 1385 and stayed faithful to Murad I.

philosophy.text: Haji Bektash Veli (c. 1209–1271) was an Islamic scholar, mystic, and philosopher from Khorasan who lived and taught in Anatolia, becoming the eponym of the Bektashi Sufi order. Alevis revere him for an Islamic understanding they see as esoteric, rational and humanistic, and consider him one of the principal teachers of Alevism.

Jalal al-Din Muhammad Rumi was born in 1207. The advancing Mongol hordes forced his family to flee west, and after years in cities across Iran, Baghdad and Damascus they settled in Konya, within the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, when he was nineteen. There he became a Sufi mystic and poet whose major work, the Masnavi, is often called a 'Qur'an in Persian.'

Yunus Emre (1238–1320) was a Turkish Sufi poet, one of the first known poets to compose in the spoken Old Anatolian Turkish. After the Sultanate of Rum's defeat at the 1243 Battle of Köse Dağ opened Anatolia to Mongol invasion, Islamic mystic literature thrived there, and Yunus Emre became one of its most distinguished poets.

Sheikh Bedreddin, born in 1359, studied theology in Konya and later traveled to Ardabil, home to the mystic Safavid order. There he embraced a pantheistic doctrine of the 'oneness of being,' which condemned divisions of religion and social class as interference in the unity of God.

Mkhitar Gosh (1130–1213), a scholar, priest and thinker regarded as a representative figure of the Armenian Renaissance, traveled from his native Gandzak to the Black Mountains of Cilicia to study theology under local priests. He later wrote a wide-ranging code of civil and canon law.

Gregory of Tatev (1346–1409 or 1410) was an Armenian philosopher and theologian educated at the monasteries of Tatev and Metzop. In his Book of Questions, completed in 1397, he defended the core principles of the Armenian Apostolic Church against Islam and the Fratres Unitores.

In Konya, Rumi's meeting with the wandering dervish Shams Tabrizi transformed the course of his life. On the night of 5 December 1248 Shams was called to the back door, went out and was never seen again. Theories hold that Rumi's youngest son killed him, that he was killed for blasphemy, or that he simply moved on. Rumi refused for more than a month to believe the rumours of his death, then after forty days accepted that Shams was dead and began dressing in black in mourning. His grief poured into the Divan of Shams Tabrizi, the beginning of his poetic output.

Gregory of Tatev wrote against uniting the Armenian church with the Dyophysite Roman Catholic Church, and composed a separate treatise against Muslims, whom medieval Armenians called Tajiks, polemically opposing Islamic teachings on prophecy and holy war. He grounded his arguments in scripture, patristic tradition, and logic.

culture.text: The Sultanate of Rum was a culturally Turco-Persian, Sunni Muslim state. The Seljuk Turks built it over conquered Byzantine territories and peoples in Anatolia after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071. It is considered the beginning of Turkish history in Anatolia.

Caravanserai were the backbone of medieval trade through Anatolia. The Sultanate of Rum developed a system of them to move trade from Iran and Central Asia. Especially strong trade ties with the Genoese formed in this period, and the increased wealth let the sultanate absorb other Turkish states.

The name Rum was a synonym for the medieval Roman Empire and its peoples, and it remains so in modern Turkish. It comes from the Aramaic and Parthian names for ancient Rome, which reached those languages through the Greek Ῥωμαῖοι (Romaioi). The Seljuk Turks used it to refer to Anatolia.
From the 12th century onward, Western European chroniclers often called Anatolia and the Sultanate of Rum Turchia. This word was the predecessor of the name Turkey.

Sultan Kayqubad I, who reigned from 1220 to 1237, is remembered for his rich architectural legacy. He is also remembered for the brilliant court culture that flourished under him. He is sometimes styled Kayqubad the Great.

After the mid-13th century Mongol invasion, people in Anatolia often looked back on Kayqubad I's reign as a golden age. The new rulers of the Anatolian beyliks even sought to justify their own authority through pedigrees traced to him.

After conquering Constantinople in 1453, the Ottoman sultans claimed to be legitimate Roman emperors. Greek aristocrats were promoted to senior administrative positions, and architecture and culture experienced profound Byzantine influence. Titles such as kayser-i rûm ("Caesar of Rome") stressed the claim.
